notation.meaning: Value of the series in period $t$

notationIntro: *The price level trends up (non-stationary); its first difference, inflation, does not trend.*

blocks.md: The price level in the US has risen almost every year since 1960: its average keeps changing, so the past says little about where it will be in ten years. Inflation — the year-to-year change in prices — instead keeps returning to familiar levels. A series like inflation, whose average and spread do not drift over time, is called stationary. Most time-series tools, including regressions of a variable on its own past, need stationary data; with trending data they can find strong but meaningless relationships. The usual fix is to look at changes instead of levels. A unit root is the case where every shock is permanent: today's value is just yesterday's plus noise, so the series wanders and never returns.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: Checking and enforcing stationarity is step one of every AR and VAR analysis in macroeconomics.
A time series $x_t$ is (weakly) **stationary** if its mean and variance are constant over time (and its autocovariances depend only on the lag). In the AR(1) model

a **unit root** is $\beta_1 = 1$: $x_t = \beta_0 + x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$, a random walk (with drift $\beta_0$), which is non-stationary. A non-stationary series can often be made stationary by **first-differencing**,

| Test | Null hypothesis | Rejecting means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dickey-Fuller | Unit root, $\beta_1 = 1$ | Evidence of stationarity |
| Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) | Unit root, allowing more lags | Evidence of stationarity |
| KPSS (Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin) | Stationary | Evidence of a unit root |
The two are paired: for a stationary series you want to **reject** in the ADF test and **fail to reject** in the KPSS test. If the data are not stationary, difference once (or twice) and test again.

- **Reading the ADF null backwards.** The null is non-stationarity; a large p-value means you cannot rule out a unit root.
- **Regressing one trending series on another.** Two unrelated random walks often show a "significant" relationship (spurious regression).
- Macroeconomic time series: preparing data for AR and VAR models; testing whether shocks to GDP or unemployment are permanent.
